paper_title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Video world models are expected to capture regularities that make visual futures predictable. Prediction errors and related scores are consequently used to assess physical plausibility and identify unexpected events [Smith et al., 2019, Piloto et al., 2022, Riochet et al., 2018, Dai et al., 2023, Garrido et al., 2025, Bordes et al., 2025, Maes et al., 2026]. Such scores also guide the selection of physically plausible generated videos [Baldassarre et al., 2025, Yuan et al., 2026]. Understanding what they measure matters when errors are used to locate events, compare videos, or reward trajectories. Let fC and fT construct context and target latent representations, also called features, from observations x. Both functions include the models encoding and token-selection steps. For predictor p, optional actions a, and scoring distance d, the prediction-error score is S(x, a) = d(p(fC(x), a), fT (x)) . This score measures prediction difficulty in the chosen representation. large value may reflect physical inconsistency, appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary model error. Physical information may also be accessible to classifier even when the predictors error responds primarily to other properties of the video. All three authors contributed equally. Preprint. We first test whether linear classifiers can distinguish physically possible from impossible events using frozen representations. We also test how well appearance information can be recovered from the same representations. IntPhys2 is synthetic video benchmark pairing physically possible events with violations such as an object passing through solid obstacle [Bordes et al., 2025]. We compare V-JEPA2-G, trained to predict latent representations, with VideoMAE2-G, trained to reconstruct masked pixels, and simple visual statistics. Linear classifiers readily recover appearance labels from all three. V-JEPA2-G provides modest advantage when classifying events as possible or impossible. We then examine how appearance and physical differences are organized across network depth. Changes in hue, brightness, and object color let us measure how far representations move, how consistently they move in the same direction across scenes, and how much those directions overlap with differences between possible and impossible events. In both V-JEPA2-G and VideoMAE2-G, appearance shifts become smaller relative to distances between unrelated videos. At deeper layers, the shifts line up more than those from randomly paired videos and overlap less with physical changes, though these trends sometimes reverse between layers. Appearance labels nevertheless remain easy to recover at the evaluated probe layers. We also test whether representation distances help predict changes in V-JEPA2-Gs prediction error. In regression analysis, they add little beyond scene conditions and simple visual statistics. Finally, we test prediction error under controlled changes to actions, appearance, motion, and physical validity. Across three action-conditioned world models, incorrect actions raise error while the observed frames are held fixed. Color changes also alter error without changing the simulated physical state. In Physion++ videos of physical interactions, repeating single frame can increase error, whereas changing color throughout clip can lower it [Tung et al., 2023]. Using Kubric, simulation and rendering framework, we test stopping and falling with and without support beneath an object [Greff et al., 2022]. Mean error is higher for stopping in both settings, even though stopping is lawful only when support is present. fixed error threshold also flags many lawful events as impossible. These results show why recoverable physical information and action sensitivity alone are insufficient to interpret prediction error as physical surprise.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Predictive video representations. Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting latent representations rather than pixels [LeCun, 2022, Bardes et al., 2024]. V-JEPA2 extends this approach to video understanding, prediction, and planning [Assran et al., 2025], while VideoMAE and VideoMAE2 learn representations through masked pixel reconstruction [Tong et al., 2022, Wang et al., 2023]. Action-conditioned models such as LeWorldModel, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WM predict visual representations from observations and actions [Maes et al., 2026, Zhou et al., 2024, Terver et al., 2026]. These objectives provide different representations and native error scales. Our comparisons retain each released pipeline and test the meaning of its error through controlled interventions. Physical information and latent geometry. Inverse-dynamics probes recover actions from video representations [Yeom et al., 2026]; robotic evaluations distinguish representations useful for reconstruction from those useful for planning [Nilaksh et al., 2026]. Layerwise probes and subspace analyses reveal physics-related structure in V-JEPA2 and VideoMAE2 [Joseph et al., 2026, Punzo et al., 2026]. Geometry regularization can improve multistep prediction [Xia et al., 2026], and PhyLatent studies physical invariance and identifiability under appearance and dynamics changes [Zeng et al., 2026]. We connect this representation-level evidence to separate question: whether measured geometry predicts native-error differences in the same model and setting. Physical prediction and violation of expectation. IntPhys and IntPhys2 evaluate possible versus impossible events [Riochet et al., 2018, Bordes et al., 2025]; Physion and Physion++ evaluate physical-outcome prediction and inference of latent physical properties [Bear et al., 2021, Tung et al., 2023]. Violation-of-expectation models use predicted-versus-observed discrepancies to identify unexpected physical events [Smith et al., 2019, Piloto et al., 2022, Dai et al., 2023, Garrido et al., 2025]. Related evaluations address counterfactual consistency and physical plausibility in generated videos [Begiristain et al., 2026, Baldassarre et al., 2025, Yuan et al., 2025, 2026]. We focus on the specificity and transfer of fixed native score: whether physical violations increase error across controlled changes in motion, appearance, and context.

sections.title: 3 Evaluation framework
sections.content: We retain each evaluated pipelines encoders, token selection, normalization, and native distance. Context-only prediction and encoding full clip before selecting context tokens are distinct computations (Section 4.2). Native score magnitudes are compared only within model. Table 1 separates evidence about representations from evidence about the score. Readout and geometry characterize encoded information; the remaining checks test predictive sensitivity and physical decisions. For threshold-based detection, lawful clip above the threshold is false alarm, and an impossible clip below it is missed violation. Table 1: Six complementary checks for interpreting prediction error as physical surprise. Calibration here means transfer of fixed decision threshold, rather than calibration of predicted probabilities. Check Readout Geometry Controlled comparison and measured property Train linear classifier on frozen representations and test it on scenes excluded from training. Measure how accurately it distinguishes physically possible from impossible events. Measure appearance and physical shifts across layers. Relative size shows how strongly appearance changes affect representations compared with differences between unrelated videos. Stronger alignment than in shuffled pairs indicates consistent response across scenes. Greater overlap than with random subspaces of the same dimension indicates shared directions between appearance and physical changes. Action Keep the observed outcome fixed and compare predictions made with correct and mismatched actions. Check whether incorrect actions increase prediction error. Appearance/static Change appearance without changing the simulated physical state, or repeat single frame throughout clip. Compare prediction error with the original clip. Physical validity Compare possible and impossible events while varying motion or appearance. Check whether impossible events consistently receive higher error within each condition. Calibration Choose an error threshold on separate calibration data and apply it unchanged to new scenes and appearances. Measure the rates of false alarms and missed violations. We evaluate V-JEPA2-G on controlled Kubric videos and IntPhys2, V-JEPA2-L on Physion++ Mass, and released action-conditioned models on TwoRoom and PushT. The IntPhys2 comparison includes VideoMAE2-G and low-level visual statistics. DINO-WM and JEPA-WM share frozen DINOv2 encoder [Oquab et al., 2024], so their comparison varies only the predictor. Uncertainty is estimated by bootstrap over independent configurations, Physion++ matched pairs within scenarios, IntPhys2 scenes, or action-test episodes. All conditions belonging to one unit remain together. Bonferroni-adjusted intervals are used for the specified families of contrasts. Thresholds and regression coefficients are fitted on data separate from evaluation. Full protocols, fitting and split histories, and reproducibility records are in the appendices. Code and numeric experiment records are available at https://github.com/3-ml/jepa-surprise (Appendix G).

sections.title: 4 Results
sections.content: 4.1 Physical-violation ordering and threshold transfer To separate physical validity from trajectory identity, we render falling sphere above either solid platform or an opening. Each setting has two continuations: the sphere stops at platform height or falls below it. Stopping is lawful on the solid platform and unsupported over the opening; falling is lawful through the opening and violates solidity when it passes through the platform. Figure 8 in the appendix shows the rendered construction. The 256 configurations cross these four cases with the original appearance, 30 hue shift throughout the clip (persistent), or the same shift starting at the target interval (abrupt), giving 3,072 clips. Stopping trajectories match across settings, as do falling trajectories. Within each setting and appearance, the two continuations share context frames and predictor outputs. Support appearance, shadows, and occlusion differ across settings. The 3 predictor observes the first 12 of 48 frames; native error is mean absolute difference from normalized EMA-target tokens for the remaining 36 frames. V-JEPA2-G gives stopping higher mean error in both settings. Consequently, impossible-minuspossible error is negative on solid support and positive over the gap (Figure 1). The native scores ordering follows the trajectory across this reversal of physical validity (Appendix Figure 9). Figure 1: V-JEPA2-G on 256 configurations. Left: impossible minus possible native error, with 98.75% configuration-bootstrap intervals adjusted for four means. The sign reverses between solid support and gap. Right: balanced accuracy under single threshold fitted on separate calibration scenes, with descriptive 95% configuration-bootstrap intervals. The dashed line marks 50%. The reversal holds under both clean and persistent-hue appearance; all four adjusted intervals exclude zero in their respective directions. Averaging the two settings would conceal the opposite orderings. Appendix E.2 reports the complete margins and intervals. single threshold fitted on 24 separate clean calibration configurations yields 53.9% balanced accuracy [52.1, 55.8] on clean evaluation clips, with equal weight to both support settings. Performance differs sharply by setting: 80.7% over gaps versus 27.1% on solid support. The threshold falsely flags about 69% of lawful clips, including every lawful solid-support continuation (Appendix Figure 10). Thus the above-chance average coexists with large false-alarm rate. Figure 1 also shows transfer under persistent and abrupt hue; Appendix E.2 gives all per-setting rates and the threshold definition. 4.2 Static-content and persistent-appearance controls We evaluate V-JEPA2-Ls full-clip masked-prediction score on the 192 official Physion++ Mass videos. The encoder processes each 16-frame window before context tokens are selected, so target frames can influence the predictor. The static diagnostic compares every complete, nonoverlapping window with versions repeating its first, middle, or last frame. These still-frame controls have higher mean error than the original videos. Across videos, the mean share of windows scoring no higher than their average static baseline is approximately 84%. The mean original-minus-static difference is negative in every scenario, and the layout-cluster sensitivity check agrees. Uncertainty is based on scenario-stratified matched pairs, with windows averaged within videos, not treated as independent observations. Repeating frames changes both content and history, so this comparison neither isolates motions causal effect nor supplies universal score correction. Persistent appearance changes can also lower error. This separate experiment uses one fixed middle 16-frame window per video. Hue shifts and pixel darkening applied throughout the window both lower mean error relative to the original and to their target-only counterparts  (Table 2)  . Changes restricted to the final four frames have uncertain original-relative effects: their adjusted intervals include zero. The persistent-versus-target-only hue ordering reverses in Collision, so the overall mean does not describe every scenario. The normalized L1 score averages spatial-token errors over the two target frame-pairs (temporal tubelets). Because the encoder sees the full window, target-only edits can affect the predictor despite unchanged context pixels. These are diagnostics of the evaluated masked-prediction implementation. Ordinary least squares (OLS) models fitted on 24 separate configurations predict physical margins (impossible minus lawful error) and appearance-induced score changes on the 256-configuration evaluation population. The baseline uses condition labels and static, motion, and shuffled-frame statistics; the expanded model adds relative representation distances and interactions with support or appearance timing. This compares geometry with information already available from the experimental conditions and visible changes. Adding final-encoder geometry changes physical-margin R2 from approximately 0.771 to 0.774, but the adjusted improvement interval includes both gains and losses. Some earlier locations worsen prediction. Here R2 uses the error of predicting the fitting-set mean as its denominator, rather than the evaluation-set mean. For appearance-score differences, both models perform worse than that reference. Across all five locations and both tasks, no improvement interval lies entirely above zero (Appendix Tables 2324). This post-hoc analysis gives limited evidence of added predictive value from the tested geometry features and linear models. Native prediction error is the world models discrepancy between predicted and observed representations; the regression error here measures how well separate model predicts differences in that discrepancy. Configuration-bootstrap intervals condition on the fitted regressions. We test 256 episodes per task or scorer under correct, zero, and reversed actions. Agent-blue blocks score higher than novel-orange blocks; block-gray agents likewise exceed matched purple. The target-only blue/orange gap is positive in 233 of 256 episodes. For target-only edits, the prediction is unchanged and differences in target-encoder shifts account for almost all of the score gaps algebraically. Role colors can carry task information. These controls therefore show that the score depends on color. They leave open whether that color information helps predict physical outcomes and whether LeWorldModel encodes task roles.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Physical labels can be read out of V-JEPA2-G representations (about 58% accuracy against 50% chance), yet its native prediction error does not consistently track physical validity in the crossedsupport test. Appearance remains decodable even as its relative displacement decreases across depth, while physical labels are modestly accessible under the evaluated probes. These findings describe the representation, but do not determine which video changes produce large native errors. The same-model regression makes that connection explicit: the selected geometry features add little predictive value beyond visual statistics and experimental conditions. 7 The native-error controls identify several sources of discrepancy. score can remain high when motion is removed, or decrease after persistent color change. In the crossed-support test, stable trajectory ordering produces opposite physical-violation orderings and poor shared-threshold performance. Abrupt recoloring asks different question: an unexpected color transition may itself violate object-property constancy. Persistent transformations remove that transition, allowing sensitivity to stable appearance change to be examined separately. In PushT, the moving lawful targets already have higher error than the static ones. Comparing absolute scores can therefore rank the action change above the hue change, even though the hue increase over its own baseline is larger. Table 5 summarizes what each setting establishes. The evaluation framework turns the broad question of physical understanding into testable claims about particular score. For physical-surprise application, the decisive checks are violation ordering within relevant conditions and false-alarm and miss rates when fixed decision rule transfers across them. These measurements connect the interpretation of prediction error to the decisions it is intended to support. sections.title: 6 Limitations
sections.content: The controlled support experiment samples one procedural family with restricted cameras, colors, and lighting. It tests transfer across those conditions only; real-world and material generalization are untested. Material appearance can convey mass or friction cues, and greater training diversity may change appearance sensitivity. Those questions require additional data and controlled model comparisons. The IntPhys2 readout and geometry-to-error transfer are post-hoc analyses. Their intervals condition on fitted models and omit refitting uncertainty; the readout also conditions on fold assignments. The tested linear geometry models do not establish mechanism or the effect of removing appearance directions. Physion++ provides contact labels and no physical-violation labels, and its full-clip scoring implementation permits target information to affect context tokens. These distinctions constrain the interpretation of each result. Model comparisons also vary architecture, pretraining, capacity, and native score. We do not estimate general limit on planning or anomaly-detection performance. Application-specific acceptable error rates were not specified. Detailed split histories, failed compatibility checks, and excluded follow-ups are retained in the appendix. Broader impact. Prediction errors can serve as measures of physical surprise when controlled tests establish what they respond to. Their use as rewards or safety signals requires validation in the intended task and environment.

Each sample uses exactly 64 decoded source frames sampled by rounded linear spacing. The four appearance conditions are clean, 90-degree hue rotation, brightness multiplier 0.45, and 180-degree selective recoloring. sections.content: C.1 Action mismatch and hue controls C.1.1 LeWorldModel, DINO-WM, and JEPA-WM controls The TwoRoom and PushT studies strict-load the released LeWorldModel checkpoints, preserve the official four-frame, frame-skip-five preprocessing and action normalization, and use 256 fresh independent episodes per task. LeWorldModel combines latent prediction with the SIGReg regularizer introduced in LeJEPA [Balestriero and LeCun, 2025]. For each episode we simulate lawful targets from the third context state under scaled five-action blocks ca for {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, render the lawful target once, and reuse the exact same target bytes under lawful ca, zero, and opposite ca action blocks. The LeWM native score is mean squared error between predicted and encoded target latents. The DINO-WM PushT extension uses the same 256 PushT episodes, target bytes, action blocks, and rendered-effect matches; it normalizes actions and proprioception with the released DINO-WM PushT statistics and scores final-step visual-latent MSE between the predictor output and encoded target. The JEPA-WM PushT extension uses the same controlled construction and threeframe teacher-forcing context with the released 224-pixel preprocessing, action and proprioception statistics, AdaLN plus RoPE predictor, and final one-step visual embedding MSE over DINOv2 patch tokens. The visual score excludes proprioceptive prediction loss, and the analysis is post-hoc exploratory. Action contrasts are same-target differences relative to the lawful-action baseline. The reported hue-minus-opposite contrasts instead subtract the opposite-action score for moving target from the hue-modified static-target score. They are absolute score comparisons across different target baselines, with predeclared rendered-effect matches. Episode-level 95% intervals use 10,000 bootstrap draws over episodes. Physion++ static and appearance diagnostics D.1 Full-population controls The fixed official Mass manifests contain 192 videos / 96 pairs: 32 pairs each in Mass-Collision, Mass-Dominoes, and Mass-Waterpush. Additional directory files do not enlarge this cohort. Every complete nonoverlapping 16-frame window is used for the static study (5,177 windows); incomplete tails are recorded and left unpadded. Each window is scored as original and with frame 0, 8, or 15 repeated throughout. The appearance study selects window n/2 from each videos complete windows, without using scores, and evaluates original, persistent hue, target-only hue, persistent darkening, and target-only darkening. Hue adds 21 PIL HSV bins modulo 256; darkening applies 4 RGB/5. Persistent transformations affect all 16 frames and target-only transformations frames 12-15. Paired future pixels/tensors match exactly; target-only context pixels/tensors match original. The exact archived scoring body uses FP16 CUDA batch-one evaluation, 12 selected context frames / four target frames, FP32 layer normalization of both operands, and mean L1 over 512 target tokens. The Transformers implementation encodes all 16 frames before selecting context tokens. Thus even target-only image changes can alter the predictor; identical future pixels under persistent/targetonly transformations need not yield identical target embeddings. This diagnostic concerns the released full-clip scoring implementation, not causal forecast conditioned only on the first 12 frames. We kept this implementation after seeing the results and did not replace it. For static results, let dvw be original minus the mean of the three static scores in window of video v. We first average dvw, or [dvw 0], within each video, then average the two videos within each matched pair. This is not an independent-window prevalence estimate. We use 50,000 scenario-stratified pair-bootstrap draws, seed 2026102601; layout-cluster sensitivity uses seed 2026102701 and 13/10/19 layout clusters. Every complete 16-frame segment was scored, yielding 273 segments. For each segment we record the native latent residual, mean consecutive absolute RGB difference on the 0-255 scale, and the fraction of pixels whose consecutive-frame change exceeds 5. For static calibration, the first, middle, or last decoded frame is repeated across all 16 input positions and rescored. The first-frame event residual is the original score minus the corresponding frozenframe score. This control does not estimate universal corrected surprise score; it asks only whether local raw peak requires temporal change. Appearance conditions rotate only the target objects post-event base color; physical conditions apply persistent target-object +z displacement of 0.25, 0.50, 1.00, or 1.50 object diameters while preserving non-target states. The scalar score is mean absolute error between predictor output and layer-normalized EMA-targetencoder tokens. sections.content: Code and numeric experiment records are available at https://github.com/3-ml/jepa-surprise/tree/local-launchers-2026-10-31. Representation and action studies: historical/results/. Crossed-support experiment: release/final256/. Physion++ controls: release/physion-static/ and release/physion-appearance/. Geometry-to-error regression: release/geometry-transfer/. Hardware, software, and recorded runtimes: docs/reproducibility.pdf. Checkpoint identities: docs/reproducibility.md. Execution instructions and required inputs: docs/LOCAL_EXECUTION.md and release/DEPENDENCIES.md. File hashes and verification: release-manifest.json and tools/check_release.py. Datasets, model weights, rendered videos, and large feature caches must be obtained separately. The execution instructions specify the required input files, software versions, and hardware.
